title: Tropical cyclone warning issued for thousands of Australians: What you need to know
text:
Serious thunderstorms, great hail, harmful winds and heavy rains for victory and NSW parts that mark a humid and stormy start of the week are forecast.
The fierce climate follows the days of heavy rains in the north of Queensland, where coastal and interior centers, including Townsville, Cardwell and Ingham, were more affected.
The communities affected by the floods to be kept up to date with the latest warnings have been urged, with fears of more rain along the way.
The Meteorology Office predicts serious thunderstorms from Dubbo to Wagga Wagga and Albury-Wodonga on the NSW-Victoria border.
Senior Dean Narramore meteorologist said the wild climate was expected since Sunday afternoon.
“We could see severe thunderstorms with large hails, harmful winds and heavy rains and that could cause sudden floods of businesses, roads and properties,” he said on Sunday.
“We could also see dangerous driving conditions with these storms, as well as damage to homes, properties and businesses, with low -electric trees and lines, particularly with those harmful winds.”
Even larger storms were expected on Monday through much of Inland NSW and the northeast of Victoria.
“We were able to see generalized falls from 25 to 50 mm in the east of Victoria and much of the center and east of Nueva de del Sur,” said Narramore.
Rain total for the north of Queensland were expected until 10 pm on Sunday, February 9, 2025.
Flood warnings occur when communities in North Western Australia remain in surveillance for a possible tropical cyclone
“And we could see even heavier falls exceeding 100 mm possible through parts of the East of Victoria and, particularly in the parts of the center and southeast of NSW.”
In Queensland, there are great flood warnings for Herbert, Burdekin, Haughton, Flinders, Cape and the Western rivers, with warning of minor than moderate warnings for a series of other basins through regions of the northeast and northwest.
Senior Meteorologist Myriam Bradbury said 24 -hour rain could reach 250 mm.
“This rain is falling on saturated land, which means that it will run quickly and overcome the already swollen rivers,” he said.
“This means that even moderate rain totals could cause rivers and could lead to dangerous flood conditions.”
Flood warnings occur when communities in North Western Australia remain in surveillance for a possible tropical cyclone.
The office said the tropical minimum near the northern coast of Kimberley could become a cyclone on Monday.
On Sunday morning it was 380 km from Broome and 160 km northwest of Kuri Bay.
“It is forecast that the bass will move to the southwest of the Kimberley coast and develop, reaching the intensity of the Cyclone on Monday,” said the office.
Wind bursts up to 100 km/h were possible along the coast between Cockatoo Island and Beagle Bay on Monday afternoon, possibly spreading more towards Broome and Bidyadanga.
A heavy rain between Cockatoo Island and Broome was also possible from Sunday.
The floods in Queensland last week forced hundreds of people to evacuate their homes and left the communities without power.
An important bridge in the city of Ingham was dragged, with Australia’s defense force called to restore temporary access for crucial supplies.
The northern Queensland has been whipped by the rain so severe that a city has left underwater, a crocodile in a garden and pub customers that need boats to drink a drink (in the photo)
Ingham residents were forced to flee from their homes, after up to 1.2 meters of rain fell. A Main Street flooded is shown
Some residents have begun to return to houses devastated by floods, with more than 4000 storms and insurance claims related to floods so far.
The total damage invoice is unknown.
Until now, $ 8 million are available for residents affected through the Commonwealth Community Aid Fund, while Queensland Prime Minister David Crisafulli is pressing so that federal support will raise the bridges above the flood level along the Bruce road.
The Executive President of the Queensland Reconstruction Authority, Jake Ellwood, warned that cleaning would be difficult, with a huge cost about the mental health of the expected affected people in addition to the physical and economic impacts.
“Recovery and reconstruction are not an event of days and weeks: it is months and years,” said the greatest retired general to journalists in Townsville on Saturday.
